title: Angada in the court
hook: Rama's last offer of peace; the foot no one can lift
carry: dharma offers peace before the fight

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama Setu, the stones that floated because they carried his name. Ram se bada Ram ka naam.
screen: `THE NAME OF GOD CARRIES WHAT WOULD SINK.`

segments.voice: Two sides lining up for a fight: a group chat, a family feud, two countries at a border. Someone has to decide whether to talk first. The army has crossed the bridge. They could attack at once. Instead, before the war starts, Rama sends one last messenger into Ravana's court with an offer: give Sita back, and there's no war. Not Hanuman, who already burned the place down. Angada. Young. Vali's son, the prince whose father Rama killed. And Angada walks alone into a golden hall full of demons, and faces the king with ten heads.
screen: `TWO SIDES LINING UP.` → `ONE LAST OFFER OF PEACE.` → `ANGADA WALKS IN ALONE.`

segments.voice: Ravana knows Angada's father died by Rama's arrow, and tries to use it: why serve the man who killed your father? Join me. Angada doesn't take it. He has chosen his side. The most famous version of this scene comes from the Ramcharitmanas, the Hindi Ramayana of Tulsidas. Angada delivers Rama's offer, and the court mocks him. So he plants one foot on the floor and says: if anyone here can move my foot, Rama will turn back. One by one, Ravana's great warriors grab his foot and heave. It doesn't move. Not an inch. Finally Ravana himself gets up from his throne and bends to grab it. And Angada pulls his foot away and says, in effect: why hold my feet? If you want to be saved, go and hold Rama's feet. Even now, the offer stands. In Valmiki's older telling the scene is different: the demons seize Angada, and he leaps up through the palace roof. But both tellings agree on what matters. Rama tried peace first. That's a real teaching of dharma. Hindu teaching on kingship lists four ways to meet an enemy: sama, talking; dana, a gift; bheda, splitting their side; and danda, force. Force comes last. Rama, God come down to set things right, still sends a messenger before he lifts his bow. Later on this path, Krishna will do the same, walking into a hostile court to ask for peace before a great war. In Hindu teaching, a war for dharma starts only after the door to peace has been held open, and refused.
screen: `RAVANA TRIES TO TURN HIM.` · `NOBODY CAN MOVE HIS FOOT.` · `RAMA TRIED PEACE FIRST.` · `SAMA FIRST. DANDA LAST.`

segments.voice: Think of a fight you're in, or about to be in: a sibling, a group chat, a coworker. Before anything else is fired, find the one sentence you'd send as your Angada: an offer of peace, said plainly, with a way back for the other side. Say it out loud once, quietly. You don't have to send it yet. Just know what it says, the way Rama did, before he ever lifted his bow.
Angada, Vali's son, who carried Rama's last offer of peace into Ravana's court, and planted a foot nobody could lift.
Your line: dharma offers peace before the fight. Even Ravana was told where to bow. That's fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Angada's foot in Ravana's court is a favorite scene of the Ramlila plays of north India, often played for both drama and laughter, and it is recited from the Lanka Kand of Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas. Both great epics send a peace mission before their war: Angada to Ravana, and later Krishna to the Kauravas.

Angada.meaning: Vali's son, a young monkey prince sent as Rama's messenger

Ravana.meaning: the ten-headed king of Lanka who took Sita

Vali.meaning: Angada's father, the monkey king killed by Rama's arrow

Ramcharitmanas.meaning: the Hindi Ramayana written by the poet Tulsidas

sama.meaning: making peace by talking, the first of the four ways

danda.meaning: force or punishment, the last of the four ways

sources.ref: Tulsidas, Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand (Angada as envoy; the planted foot)
Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Angada as envoy, roughly sarga 41)
the four means (upaya) of dealing with an enemy: sama, dana, bheda, danda, in Hindu texts on kingship (e.g. Manusmriti 7; Arthashastra)
Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Krishna's peace mission to the Kaurava court)
